criteria.name: Report presentation
criteria.reasoning: The report has a logical structure, executive summary, headings and a generally understandable style. Grammar and wording have recurring flaws, and the bibliography is not professionally presented. Wikipedia is cited despite being disallowed, and launch-table citations such as [49]–[55] do not match the listed bibliography.

evidence.quote: This report outlines the intended designs and procedures involved in the construction of a Earth observation satellite – specifically for coral reef and ocean monitoring.

technical_issues.issue: The stated 87.79° inclination is prograde and cannot provide the required positive sun-synchronous nodal precession. A circular orbit near 600 km requires a retrograde inclination of roughly 97.8° under the usual J2 model.
The orbital-element table gives a = 7171 km, but with the stated 6371 km Earth radius and 600 km altitude, a should be approximately 6971 km.
RAAN is not determined by the launch facility's location as claimed. The selected launch time and orbital-plane geometry determine the achievable RAAN.
Kourou is at approximately 5° N, not 45.05° N. The reported latitude is incorrect.
The reported mean access duration of 580.786 seconds is about 9.7 minutes, not almost 20 minutes.

A sun-synchronous orbit does not inherently provide continuous sunlight to the spacecraft, nor does it guarantee that the descending orbit segment is sunlit. Local time of node and eclipse geometry are not specified.
The report generalizes that launch vehicles inject passenger satellites into the same orbit. Rideshare deployments may use different orbits through separate deployment stages or propulsion.
The drag-sail EOL proposal lacks sail sizing, decay-time analysis and demonstration that the satellite will meet a disposal timescale or reliably burn up.

Access windows alone do not establish communications performance. No link budget, radio-frequency compatibility, antenna constraints or confirmation that the observatory is configured as a spacecraft ground station is provided.
The report does not give payload resolution, swath or viewing geometry to show that the proposed instrument can conduct the required fluid-lensing imaging from the selected orbit.

overall: The report is structured and covers most mission elements, but major errors in the sun-synchronous orbit definition and supporting calculations undermine the design. Weighted result from the criterion marks: 45/100.

feedback.summary: You present a clear coral-reef monitoring concept and cover most mission elements, with a logical report structure and STK access figures. The main limitation is that key orbit values and interpretations are inconsistent, weakening confidence in the design. Strengthen the technical evidence, clarify who operates the mission and who uses its data, and make your conclusions reflect what the analysis does—and does not—demonstrate.
next_steps: Rework the Orbit section using a consistent set of orbital elements: check the 600 km semi-major axis, use a retrograde inclination of about 97.8° for sun-synchronous precession, and explain how launch timing and orbital-plane geometry set RAAN. Verify the launch-site latitude and distinguish access duration from the number of daily contacts.

Build evidence that the mission will work: add payload resolution, swath and viewing geometry; a communications link budget and frequency/antenna compatibility; and a sized drag sail with a disposal-time analysis. Correct the interpretation of the 580.786-second access duration, and include relevant STK project files if available.

Revise the Introduction, Conclusion and presentation together: explicitly identify the operator and customer groups, qualify conclusions against the orbit and performance evidence, and check grammar, citation matching and bibliography quality. Replace unsupported or unsuitable references with appropriate sources.

criteria.C1: Your Introduction explains the coral-reef monitoring need, identifies marine and conservation scientists as users, and justifies using one spacecraft. To reach the next level, clearly name the mission operator and distinguish it from customer or user groups, with complete supporting references.
criteria.C2: Your Launch, Orbit and Ground Control & Communications sections cover the main design elements, and Images 1–5 provide STK access evidence. However, the stated 87.79° inclination cannot provide sun-synchronous precession; correct the orbit elements and support payload, link and EOL performance. Clarify access timing and provide the relevant STK files.
criteria.C3: Your Conclusion usefully recaps the proposed design, but mostly summarizes it and presents consistent illumination too definitively. To reach the next level, draw specific conclusions from validated orbit and performance evidence, and identify limitations where the analysis does not establish mission capability.
criteria.C4: Your report has an Executive Summary, logical headings and a generally understandable structure. For a more professional standard, edit recurring grammar and wording issues, present the Bibliography consistently, and ensure every in-text citation matches a suitable listed source; the launch citations and Wikipedia reference need attention.
